content:
Quick answer: Recovering from arthritis fatigue usually takes a gradual plan, not a single fix. Rule out treatable causes with your GP, find a daily activity level you can manage even on a bad day, add planned rests, protect your sleep, then build activity by small steps each week. Expect ups and downs, and adjust rather than push through.

Arthritis fatigue is not ordinary tiredness. It can feel like a heavy, drained exhaustion that a good night's sleep does not fix, and it can affect your concentration, mood and ability to do everyday things. Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) describes fatigue as a common and often difficult symptom of many types of arthritis. If you are coming out of a flare, a period of illness or a long spell of exhaustion, this guide gives you a structured, four-week plan to rebuild your energy gradually. For background on why fatigue happens, read arthritis fatigue explained; for causes and when to see your GP, see managing arthritis fatigue.

Before you start: check for treatable causes

Fatigue in arthritis often has more than one driver, and some of them can be treated. Before or alongside this plan, it is worth talking to your GP or rheumatology team, especially if fatigue is new, getting worse or very severe. They may consider:

  • Active inflammation. In rheumatoid and other inflammatory arthritis, fatigue is often worse when the disease is active. NICE's rheumatoid arthritis guideline (NG100) recognises fatigue as part of the condition and supports treating to control disease activity.
  • Anaemia. Low iron or other types of anaemia are common in inflammatory arthritis and can cause tiredness and breathlessness. The NHS lists tiredness and lack of energy as common symptoms of iron deficiency anaemia.
  • Thyroid problems, low vitamin D, diabetes or other conditions, which a blood test can check.
  • Medicines. Some medicines, including some painkillers and those that affect sleep, can cause drowsiness.
  • Sleep problems, such as pain waking you at night, insomnia or sleep apnoea.
  • Low mood, depression or anxiety, which are common with long-term pain and closely linked to fatigue.

The plan below works alongside medical treatment, not instead of it.

How the four-week plan works

The plan is built on approaches widely used by NHS occupational therapists and physiotherapists: understanding your energy, pacing, planned rest, good sleep and gradually building activity. It avoids two common traps:

  • Boom and bust: doing a lot on a good day, then crashing for several days afterwards.
  • Too much rest: resting so much that fitness drops, which makes everyday tasks more tiring and fatigue worse.
WeekFocusMain goal
1Observe and stabiliseFind your baseline and stop the crashes
2Rest and sleepAdd planned rests and a steady sleep routine
3Gentle buildIncrease activity by small, planned steps
4ConsolidateAdd what matters to you and plan for setbacks

Four weeks is a starting framework, not a deadline. Many people take longer, and that is fine. Move to the next week only when the current one feels manageable.

Week 1: observe and stabilise

Keep a simple energy diary

For seven days, note what you do in blocks across the day and rate your energy from 0 (exhausted) to 10 (full of energy) morning, afternoon and evening. Note your sleep, pain and anything that drained or boosted you. Our pain tracking journal can be adapted for this.

Find your baseline

Your baseline is the amount of activity you can manage on a bad day as well as a good one, without crashing afterwards. Look at your diary. If you walked for 20 minutes on a good day and crashed, but 8 minutes was fine even on a poor day, your walking baseline is around 8 minutes. Do the same for other key activities, such as housework, computer time or standing to cook. It is better to start too low than too high.

Stop the crashes

  • Stick to your baseline every day this week, even if you feel able to do more.
  • Spread essential tasks across the day and week rather than doing them all at once.
  • Cancel or postpone anything that is not essential.
  • Ask for help with heavy tasks such as shopping, cleaning and gardening.

Week 2: planned rest and better sleep

Plan rests before you need them

Planned rests are short breaks taken at set times, before you are exhausted, not collapses after you have done too much. Aim for:

  • Two or three short rests through the day, of around 10 to 20 minutes each
  • A rest that is genuinely restful: sitting or lying quietly, breathing slowly, listening to calm music, rather than scrolling on your phone
  • Avoiding long daytime naps, which can disrupt night-time sleep; if you need to nap, keep it short and before mid-afternoon

Build a steady sleep routine

  • Get up at around the same time each day, including weekends.
  • Wind down for an hour before bed, with screens off and lights low.
  • Keep your bedroom dark, quiet and comfortable.
  • Cut down on caffeine in the afternoon and evening, and on alcohol.
  • Manage night pain with pillows, warmth and pain relief timed as your GP or pharmacist advises. See our guides to sleeping with arthritis and sleep positions for every joint.

Keep your baseline steady

Do not increase activity yet. Keep to your week 1 baseline while rests and sleep settle.

Week 3: build activity gently

Increase by small steps

Choose one or two activities and increase them by a small amount, often suggested as around 10 to 20 per cent, for example from 8 minutes of walking to 9 or 10. Keep the increase for several days. If you cope without a crash, increase again. If you crash, go back to the previous level for a while.

Add gentle exercise

Regular physical activity is one of the most helpful things for arthritis and often helps fatigue over time, even though it can feel like the last thing you want to do. Start gently:

  • Short walks, building up slowly
  • Seated or standing exercises at home; our exercise hub has routines
  • Gentle strengthening, as stronger muscles make everyday tasks less tiring
  • Warm-water exercise, tai chi or gentle yoga, if available locally

The NHS physical activity guidelines suggest building towards 150 minutes of moderate activity a week plus strengthening on two days, but that is a long-term goal, not a week-3 target. Start where you are.

Use pacing tools

  • Break tasks into smaller chunks with short rests between.
  • Sit to do tasks such as ironing, preparing vegetables or getting dressed.
  • Alternate heavy and light tasks, and physical and mental ones.
  • Use labour-saving gadgets and an online shopping delivery.

Our guide to how to pace activities properly explains these tools step by step.

Week 4: consolidate and add what matters

Add something you enjoy

Fatigue often squeezes out the activities that make life enjoyable, such as seeing friends, hobbies or going out. Once essentials are manageable, plan in one enjoyable activity each week, kept within your energy budget. Enjoyment and connection matter for mood, which in turn affects fatigue.

Plan your week

At the start of each week, look at what is coming up. Spread demanding activities out, plan rest around them, and leave some space for the unexpected. Many people find it helpful to think of energy as a budget: spend it on what matters most, and save some in reserve.

Plan for setbacks

Setbacks are normal. Flares, infections, poor nights or stressful events can knock energy back. Write a short setback plan:

  • Go back to your week 1 or 2 level for a few days
  • Keep planned rests and your sleep routine
  • Keep up a little gentle movement rather than stopping completely
  • Build back up gradually when things settle
  • Contact your GP or rheumatology team if a setback lasts or comes with a flare. See our flare-up guide.

Food, drink and fatigue

  • Eat regular meals; skipping meals can make energy dip.
  • Aim for a balanced diet with plenty of vegetables, fruit, wholegrains and protein. Batch cook on better days.
  • Drink enough fluids through the day.
  • Limit alcohol, which affects sleep and mood.
  • There is no good evidence that any supplement cures arthritis fatigue. If you are concerned about iron or vitamin levels, ask your GP for a blood test rather than taking supplements blindly.

Mood, stress and fatigue

Fatigue, pain and low mood are closely linked, and each can make the others worse. Helpful steps include talking to people you trust, relaxation and breathing techniques, and gentle activity outdoors. If you feel low or anxious most days, speak to your GP. In England, you can also refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, contact your GP, call NHS 111, or call Samaritans free on 116 123.

Fatigue at work

If fatigue affects your work, talk to your employer about reasonable adjustments, such as flexible hours, a phased return after sickness, more breaks or working from home on some days. Arthritis can count as a disability under the Equality Act 2010. Access to Work may be able to help with support or equipment. Our guide to the Access to Work scheme explains how to apply.

Getting extra support

  • Occupational therapy: occupational therapists help people manage everyday tasks with less effort. The NHS explains how to get a referral, which may be through your GP, rheumatology team or local council.
  • Physiotherapy: for help building up activity safely. Many areas allow self-referral.
  • Rheumatology nurse or advice line: if fatigue may be linked to active disease or medicines.
  • Self-management courses: some local NHS services and charities run courses for people living with long-term conditions.

When to get medical help

  • See your GP if fatigue is new, getting worse, not improving after a few weeks of pacing and rest, or stopping you doing everyday activities.
  • See your GP soon if fatigue comes with unexplained weight loss, fevers, night sweats, breathlessness, or feeling faint.
  • Contact your rheumatology team if fatigue comes with more joint swelling or stiffness, which may mean your arthritis is active.
  • Contact your GP or rheumatology team the same day if you feel unwell with signs of infection while on immune-suppressing medicines.
  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathlessness or signs of a stroke.

How long does it take to recover from arthritis fatigue?

It varies widely. Some people notice improvement within a few weeks of pacing, planned rest and better sleep; others take months, especially if inflammation, anaemia or low mood also need treating. Progress is often gradual with ups and downs, so judge it over weeks rather than days.

Should I rest or exercise with arthritis fatigue?

Both, in balance. Planned, short rests help, but too much rest reduces fitness and can make fatigue worse. Start gentle activity at a level you can manage even on a bad day, and build up by small steps.

What is boom and bust?

Boom and bust is doing a lot on a good day, then crashing for days afterwards. It is very common with fatigue and pain. Pacing, which means doing a steady, planned amount each day and building up gradually, helps break the cycle.

Can blood tests explain my tiredness?

Sometimes. Your GP may check for anaemia, thyroid problems, vitamin D levels, diabetes and markers of inflammation. Finding and treating a cause can help, but fatigue in arthritis often has several contributors, so self-management usually matters too.

Is arthritis fatigue a sign my arthritis is getting worse?

Not always, but in inflammatory arthritis fatigue is often worse when the disease is active. If fatigue comes with more swollen, stiff or painful joints, contact your rheumatology team, as your treatment may need reviewing.

Will supplements help my energy?

There is no good evidence that any supplement cures arthritis fatigue. If you are concerned about low iron, vitamin B12 or vitamin D, ask your GP about a blood test. In the UK, the NHS advises everyone to consider vitamin D in autumn and winter.
